title: Grade 9
emphasis: Advanced nuance, rhetoric, and abstract concepts

words.definition: dealing with problems in a practical, realistic way rather than following theory or ideals

hero.text: Instead of waiting for the perfect plan, Juniper took a pragmatic approach: she fixed the leak with what she had and planned a full repair later.

words.everyday: The student council made a pragmatic choice to hold the dance in the gym, since the budget could not cover a rented hall.

contrast.nonExample: Theo refused to start his essay until he found a topic that would change the world.
contrast.explanation: Theo is guided by an ideal, not by what will actually work. A pragmatic person focuses on realistic results.

items.prompt: What does "pragmatic" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: The mayor took a pragmatic approach, choosing the plan the city could actually afford over the one that looked best on paper.

options.text: focused on what is popular with voters
focused on what works in real conditions
focused on the most ambitious goal

wrong.a: Popularity is not mentioned; the deciding factor was cost.
wrong.c: Tradition is not the reason given.
wrong.d: The ambitious plan is the one "on paper" that she rejected.

items.hint: Notice the contrast: "could actually afford" versus "looked best on paper."
items.explanation: Pragmatic means practical and realistic. The mayor picked the plan that would work with real money, not the ideal one.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: The scientists wanted a perfect experiment, but with only two weeks of funding left, they made the ___ decision to test the three most promising samples instead of all twenty.

wrong.b: Reckless means careless about risk; their choice was careful.
wrong.c: Sentimental means driven by emotion, which the passage does not show.
wrong.a: Theoretical is the opposite: about ideas rather than practice.

items.hint: The limits of time and money forced a realistic adjustment.
items.explanation: "Only two weeks of funding left" shows a real-world limit. Testing the three best samples is a pragmatic, workable compromise.
items.clue: only two weeks of funding left; instead of all twenty

items.prompt: Which word best describes Coach Rivera's decision?
items.passage: Coach Rivera believed every player deserved equal time, but in the championship game she kept her strongest five on the court, explaining, "Today, we play to win."

wrong.c: Cynical means doubting others' motives; she is not doubting anyone.
wrong.a: Hypocritical implies dishonesty; she openly explains her choice.
wrong.b: Impulsive means acting without thought; she gives a reason.

items.hint: She sets aside a belief because of the real situation, and she explains why calmly.
items.explanation: Pragmatic fits: she adjusts her ideal to the practical demands of the moment. Hypocritical suggests pretending to hold a belief, and cynical suggests distrust of people, which the passage does not show.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what pragmatic means.

chunks.text: Rather than wait for a new building,
the pragmatic principal
turned the unused library corner into a study room.
demanded a grand new campus before any classes resumed.

items.hint: A pragmatic person uses what is available to solve the problem now.
items.explanation: Turning an existing space into a study room is a realistic, workable solution. Demanding a grand campus first is idealistic, the opposite of pragmatic.

items.prompt: Which speaker uses "pragmatic" correctly?

options.text: "The poem was so pragmatic that it made me cry about the ocean."
"Let's be pragmatic: we can't paint the whole mural by Friday, so let's finish one wall well."
"He gave a pragmatic shout when his team scored."
"That idea is pragmatic because nobody has ever tried anything like it."

items.hint: Pragmatic describes a realistic, practical way of handling a problem.
items.explanation: Scaling the mural down to what can really be finished is pragmatic. The other lines use the word for emotion, loudness, or originality, none of which mean practical.

words.definition: to support a claim with evidence that shows it is true

hero.text: Pixel substantiated her claim that the signal came from the old tower by showing the map, the timestamps, and the recording.

words.everyday: In her history essay, Ana substantiated her argument about the causes of the war with quotes from three primary sources.

contrast.nonExample: Marcus kept repeating, louder each time, that his team was the best in the league.
contrast.explanation: Repeating a claim, even loudly, does not substantiate it. To substantiate, you must provide evidence.

items.prompt: Does this person substantiate the claim?
items.passage: Lin says the new bus route saves time. To show it, she presents a chart of arrival times from three weeks before and three weeks after the change.
items.hint: Ask: did she give evidence, or just an opinion?
items.explanation: Yes. A chart of real arrival times is evidence that supports her claim, so she substantiates it.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: The reporter's editor refused to publish the accusation until the reporter could ___ it with documents or at least two reliable witnesses.

wrong.a: Exaggerating makes a claim bigger, not better supported.
wrong.c: Summarizing shortens; it adds no proof.
wrong.d: Announcing is exactly what the editor will not allow yet.

items.hint: What do documents and witnesses do for an accusation?
items.explanation: Documents and witnesses are evidence, and evidence is what substantiates a claim. Announcing or summarizing it would not make it more trustworthy.
items.clue: documents or at least two reliable witnesses

items.prompt: Which word means the OPPOSITE of "substantiate" in this sentence?
items.passage: New fossil finds substantiated the theory that the two species lived at the same time.

wrong.b: Confirmed is close in meaning, not opposite.
wrong.d: Described is neutral; it neither proves nor disproves.
wrong.a: Inspired is unrelated to proof.

items.hint: Look for a word meaning "showed it was false."
items.explanation: Substantiate means support with evidence. Refute means prove false, the opposite. Confirmed is a near-synonym.

items.prompt: "Substantiate" is related to "substance" (something solid and real). How does that help explain the word?

options.text: to remove a claim from a discussion
to put a claim in simpler words
to make a claim sound more exciting
to give a claim solid, real support

items.hint: Something with substance has real weight.
items.explanation: Substantiating a claim gives it substance: solid evidence that makes it real and believable.

items.prompt: Which word best describes what the class did?
items.passage: Mr. Okafor's students claimed the school's recycling bins were often misused. Over two weeks they sorted and weighed the bins' contents, then photographed the results for the principal.

wrong.d: Speculating is guessing; they gathered evidence instead.
wrong.b: Dramatizing means making something theatrical.
wrong.c: Protesting objects to something; the focus here is on proof.

items.hint: The students collected data to back up their claim.
items.explanation: Weighing and photographing the contents produced evidence for their claim, so they substantiated it. Speculating is guessing without evidence.
items.clue: sorted and weighed; photographed the results

words.definition: unclear or open to more than one meaning, often on purpose to avoid committing

hero.text: When Rex asked if the mission was safe, Bolt gave an equivocal answer: "Well, it depends how you define safe."

words.everyday: Asked whether she supported the new law, the senator gave an equivocal reply that both sides claimed as agreement.

contrast.nonExample: When asked if he broke the vase, Leo said, "Yes, I did, and I'm sorry."
contrast.explanation: Leo's answer is direct and has only one meaning. An equivocal answer is vague or can be read two ways.

items.prompt: What does "equivocal" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: The study's results were equivocal: some data suggested the drug helped, while other data suggested it did nothing.

options.text: open to more than one interpretation

items.hint: The data point in two different directions.
items.explanation: Equivocal means unclear or open to more than one reading. Some data said yes and some said no, so the results did not give a clear answer.

items.prompt: Which word best describes the spokesperson's statement?
items.passage: Asked whether layoffs were coming, the company spokesperson said, "We are always evaluating our options," a phrase that could mean yes, no, or not yet.

wrong.a: An honest answer would state what is actually planned.
wrong.b: Nothing in the reply is aggressive.
wrong.d: Eloquent describes graceful speech; this reply is just slippery.

items.hint: The phrase "could mean yes, no, or not yet."
items.explanation: A statement that could mean several things, used to avoid a commitment, is equivocal. Eloquent means beautifully expressed, which is about style, not clarity.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: Critics found the novel's ending deliberately ___: readers still argue about whether the narrator survived or only imagined her escape.
items.hint: If readers argue about what happened, how clear is the ending?
items.explanation: "Readers still argue" about two possible meanings, so the ending is equivocal. Predictable would leave nothing to argue about.
items.clue: readers still argue about whether

items.prompt: Which word means the OPPOSITE of "equivocal" in this sentence?
items.passage: The witness's equivocal testimony did little to help either side of the case.
items.hint: Find the word meaning "having only one clear meaning."
items.explanation: Equivocal means open to more than one meaning. Unambiguous means having one clear meaning, the opposite. Uncertain is close to equivocal.

items.prompt: Which reply is the most equivocal?
items.passage: Maya asks her friend, "Will you come to my recital on Saturday?"

options.text: "Sorry, I have a game that day."
"I can't wait to hear you play."
"Yes! I'll be in the front row."

items.hint: Which answer avoids saying yes or no?
items.explanation: "We'll see how things go" commits to nothing and can be read either way, so it is equivocal. The other replies give a clear yes or no.

words.definition: seeming to be everywhere at the same time; extremely common

hero.text: After Nova saved the city, her lightning logo became ubiquitous, appearing on posters, backpacks, and every bus stop.

words.everyday: Smartphones have become so ubiquitous that it is hard to find a public place where no one is using one.

contrast.nonExample: Only one shop in town sells the rare blue cheese, and it is often sold out.
contrast.explanation: Something rare and hard to find is the opposite of ubiquitous. Ubiquitous things turn up everywhere.

items.prompt: What does "ubiquitous" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: Plastic is now so ubiquitous that scientists have found tiny pieces of it in Arctic ice and on the deep ocean floor.

wrong.a: Plastic may be harmful, but the sentence is about where it is found.
wrong.c: Plastic is not new; the point is how widespread it is.
wrong.d: Cost is never mentioned.

items.hint: Arctic ice and the deep ocean are very far apart. What does that tell you?
items.explanation: Ubiquitous means found nearly everywhere. Plastic turning up even in remote places shows how widespread it is.

items.prompt: Is the item described ubiquitous?
items.passage: In the 1800s, a handful of wealthy families in one city owned telephones, and most people had never seen one.
items.hint: Was the telephone everywhere, or rare?
items.explanation: No. Owned by only a few families and unseen by most people, the early telephone was rare, not ubiquitous.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: In the 1950s, television antennas became ___ in American suburbs; from any rooftop, you could see dozens of them stretching down the street.
items.hint: Dozens on every street suggests they were very common.
items.explanation: "Dozens of them stretching down the street" shows antennas were everywhere, so they were ubiquitous. Obsolete would mean out of use, the opposite.
items.clue: dozens of them stretching down the street

items.prompt: Which word best fits the description?
items.passage: Coffee shops in this city are on nearly every corner, in train stations, inside bookstores, and even in the hospital lobby.

wrong.d: Popular says people like them, not that they are everywhere.
wrong.b: Abundant means plentiful, close but weaker; ubiquitous highlights appearing in every setting.
wrong.c: Fashionable is about trends, not location.

items.hint: The focus is on how they appear in every kind of place.
items.explanation: Ubiquitous stresses being everywhere at once, which matches shops on corners, stations, bookstores, and hospitals. Popular means well liked, and fashionable means trendy; neither says where they are found.

items.prompt: Which word fits the description of the dandelions?
items.passage: By late May the dandelions had spread across the soccer fields, sprouted through cracks in the parking lot, and even appeared in the planters on the school roof.
items.hint: Count the places the dandelions appeared.
items.explanation: Showing up on fields, in pavement cracks, and on the roof means the dandelions were everywhere: ubiquitous. Endangered would mean nearly gone, the opposite.
items.clue: soccer fields; cracks in the parking lot; planters on the school roof

words.definition: to accept or agree to something quietly, often without really wanting to

hero.text: Kai wanted to keep searching all night, but he acquiesced when the team voted to rest until dawn.

words.everyday: After a long debate, the band finally acquiesced to the drummer's request to play the song more slowly.

contrast.nonExample: Rosa argued loudly against the new rule and organized a petition to overturn it.
contrast.explanation: Rosa actively resists. Acquiescing means going along with something without resistance.

items.prompt: Which person acquiesces?

options.text: Hana sighs but agrees to her brother's choice of movie.
Omar storms out when the plan changes.
Bea suggests three new ideas for the trip.
Dev insists on choosing the restaurant himself.

items.hint: Look for someone who goes along with something without fighting it.
items.explanation: Hana is not thrilled (she sighs) but quietly agrees. That is acquiescing. Dev and Omar resist, and Bea is proposing, not accepting.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: The king had hoped to keep his full powers, but facing a united army of nobles in 1215, he was forced to ___ to their demands and seal the Magna Carta.

wrong.b: Objecting is resisting, the opposite of what happened.
wrong.c: Retaliating means striking back.
wrong.d: Appealing means asking for a different decision.

items.hint: He did not want to, but he had to go along.
items.explanation: "Had hoped to keep" and "forced to" show he gave in reluctantly. Acquiesce means to accept without further resistance.
items.clue: had hoped to keep; forced to

items.prompt: Which word best describes how the city council responded?
items.passage: The council had opposed the skate park for years. When hundreds of residents signed a petition, the council quietly approved the funding without further debate.

wrong.b: Nothing shows the council was happy about it.
wrong.d: Retreated suggests backing away physically or in battle, a rougher fit.
wrong.a: Collaborating means working together as partners; they simply gave in.

items.hint: They stopped opposing and went along, without enthusiasm.
items.explanation: Acquiesced fits: the council accepted the demand quietly, after resisting. Celebrated suggests joy, and collaborated suggests actively working together, neither of which is described.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what acquiesce means.

chunks.text: Although she preferred blue,
Lucia acquiesced
and painted the room the green her sister wanted.
and refused to touch a brush until blue was chosen.

items.hint: To acquiesce is to go along despite your own preference.
items.explanation: Lucia gives up her preference and goes along with her sister: acquiescing. Refusing to paint is resistance, the opposite.

items.prompt: Which word is closest in meaning to "acquiesced" in this sentence?
items.passage: Tired of arguing, the students acquiesced to the teacher's choice of book for the final project.

wrong.a: Rejoiced means celebrated; they were tired of arguing, not joyful.
wrong.b: Challenged is what they stopped doing.
wrong.c: Volunteering is eager; acquiescing is reluctant.

items.hint: They went along with it after arguing.
items.explanation: Complied means went along with a request or rule, which matches acquiesced. Volunteered suggests eagerness, but acquiescing is reluctant.

words.definition: to warn or scold someone firmly but without great anger

hero.text: Juniper gently admonished the new recruits for leaving the lab door unlocked overnight.

words.everyday: The librarian admonished the students to keep their voices down during exam week.

contrast.nonExample: The coach praised the team for their hard work during practice.
contrast.explanation: Praise is the opposite of admonishing. To admonish is to warn or correct someone about a fault.

items.prompt: Is this an example of admonishing?
items.passage: Mr. Chen took Zara aside and firmly reminded her that copying a classmate's homework was not acceptable and could not happen again.
items.hint: Is he warning or correcting her about a fault?
items.explanation: Yes. A firm warning about wrong behavior is an admonishment. He corrects her seriously but without shouting.

items.prompt: Which word best describes what the doctor did?
items.passage: The doctor looked over Jamal's x-ray and said seriously, "If you keep skateboarding without a helmet, next time it could be much worse."

wrong.d: She is not trying to hurt his feelings.
wrong.a: Consoling would be comforting, not warning.
wrong.b: Interrogating means questioning closely.

items.hint: She is giving a serious warning about his behavior.
items.explanation: The doctor warns Jamal about a risky habit: she admonishes him. Insulting means being rude to hurt someone, and consoling means comforting.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: In the fable, the old tortoise ___ the young hare, warning him that speed without patience would someday cost him the race.
items.hint: The clue is "warning him" about a fault.
items.explanation: "Warning him" about his impatience is the key clue. To admonish is to warn or reprove. Flattering is praising too much, the opposite tone.
items.clue: warning him

items.prompt: Which word means the OPPOSITE of "admonished" in this sentence?
items.passage: The principal admonished the class for the mess left in the cafeteria.
items.hint: Look for a word that means praised.
items.explanation: Admonished means warned or scolded. Commended means praised, the opposite. Reprimanded is a near-synonym, though usually harsher.

items.prompt: Which line is the speaker most clearly admonishing someone?

options.text: "I wonder what we're having for dinner."
"Can you pass me the scissors, please?"
"Remember, if you leave the oven on again, someone could get hurt."

items.hint: Find the line that gives a firm warning about a fault.
items.explanation: Warning someone not to repeat a careless mistake is admonishing. The other lines praise, request, or wonder.

words.definition: to refer to something indirectly, without naming it outright

hero.text: Bolt never mentioned the failed rescue by name, but he alluded to it when he said, "We all remember what happened at the bridge."

words.everyday: The poem alludes to the story of Icarus when it describes a boy who flew too close to the sun.

contrast.nonExample: In his speech, the principal said, "Last year's flood damaged the gym floor."
contrast.explanation: The principal names the event directly. To allude is to hint at something without stating it plainly.

items.prompt: What does "alluded" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: Without saying her name, the speaker alluded to the famous scientist by mentioning "the woman who won two Nobel Prizes."
items.hint: "Without saying her name" is the key clue.
items.explanation: Alluding means referring to something without naming it outright. The speaker hints at the scientist through a detail instead of her name.

items.prompt: Which statement about the passage is true?
items.passage: In his novel, the author describes a character who must choose between "two roads that diverged in a wood," a clear nod to a well-known poem by Robert Frost.

options.text: The author denies knowing the poem.
The author quotes the entire poem.
The author alludes to Frost's poem.

items.hint: A "nod" is an indirect reference.
items.explanation: Borrowing a famous phrase as "a nod" to a poem is an allusion. The author alludes to Frost's work without retelling it.
items.clue: a clear nod to

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: Although the senator never named her opponent, everyone understood whom she meant when she ___ to "a certain candidate who missed half the votes last year."
items.hint: She refers to him, but only indirectly.
items.explanation: "Never named" but "everyone understood whom she meant" is the definition of alluding: an indirect reference.
items.clue: never named her opponent; whom she meant

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what allude means.

chunks.text: The film's title
alludes to a Greek myth
without ever naming the hero it is based on.
by printing the myth's full text in the opening credits.

items.hint: Alluding is indirect. Which ending keeps the reference indirect?
items.explanation: Referring to a myth "without ever naming the hero" is an allusion. Printing the full text is a direct reference, not an allusion.

items.prompt: Is this an example of alluding?
items.passage: At lunch, Priya said to her friend, "So, are you going to tell me what happened with the science fair, or should I ask Ms. Patel?"
items.hint: Does Priya refer to the event indirectly or name it outright?
items.explanation: No. Priya names the science fair directly. Alluding would mean hinting, for example "Are you going to tell me about last Friday?"

words.definition: similar in a way that allows a useful comparison

hero.text: Pixel explained that the city's power grid is analogous to a body's blood vessels: both carry energy to every part of the system.

words.everyday: A bird's wing and a bat's wing are analogous structures: they do the same job but developed separately.

contrast.nonExample: The red apple and the green apple are both apples.
contrast.explanation: Two things of the same kind are simply alike. Analogous describes different things that share a meaningful similarity useful for comparison.

items.prompt: What does "analogous" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: The teacher said a cell membrane is analogous to a security gate, since both control what enters and leaves.
items.hint: A cell and a gate are very different, yet they share something.
items.explanation: Analogous means similar in a way that supports a comparison. Membranes and gates both control what passes through.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: Historians sometimes argue that the spread of the printing press is ___ to the rise of the internet: each made information cheaper and harder to control.

wrong.a: Identical overstates it; a press and the internet are clearly not the same thing.
wrong.b: Superior means better, which the passage does not argue.
wrong.d: Unrelated contradicts the shared effect described.

items.hint: The two are different technologies with a shared effect.
items.explanation: The shared effect ("each made information cheaper") makes the comparison useful, so analogous fits. Identical would mean exactly the same, which is too strong.
items.clue: each made information cheaper and harder to control

items.prompt: Which word best completes the sentence?
items.passage: A referee in a soccer game plays a role ___ to a judge in a courtroom: both enforce rules impartially.
items.hint: They are not the same job, but they share a key feature.
items.explanation: Analogous fits because refereeing and judging differ in many ways but share one important feature. Identical is too strong, and opposite contradicts "both enforce rules."

items.prompt: Which word is closest in meaning to "analogous" in this sentence?
items.passage: The way a thermostat keeps a room warm is analogous to the way sweating keeps your body cool.
items.hint: Which word suggests two things working in a similar way?
items.explanation: Parallel means similar in a corresponding way, like analogous. Both systems respond to temperature to keep things stable.

items.prompt: Which word best describes the relationship the writer draws?
items.passage: In her essay, Kim argued that training for a marathon is like writing a novel: both require small daily efforts, stubborn patience, and a willingness to push through boring middle stretches.
items.hint: "Is like" and "both require" signal a comparison.
items.explanation: Kim compares two different activities by their shared demands, so she presents them as analogous. Contradictory would mean they conflict.
items.clue: is like; both require

words.definition: the direct opposite of something, or a contrast of opposite ideas placed side by side

hero.text: Rex's calm, careful planning is the antithesis of Bolt's rush-in-first style.

words.everyday: Charles Dickens begins A Tale of Two Cities with an antithesis: "It was the best of times, it was the worst of times."

contrast.nonExample: Ella's sneakers and her sister's sneakers are slightly different shades of white.
contrast.explanation: A slight difference is not an antithesis. An antithesis is a complete or striking opposite.

items.prompt: What does "antithesis" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: The noisy, crowded city was the antithesis of the quiet farm where she grew up.
items.hint: Compare "noisy, crowded" with "quiet."
items.explanation: An antithesis is the direct opposite. Noisy and crowded are the opposite of quiet and peaceful.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: The dictator claimed to defend freedom, yet his secret police and censored newspapers were the very ___ of freedom.
items.hint: "Yet" signals a contrast. Are secret police and censorship part of freedom, or its opposite?
items.explanation: Secret police and censorship directly oppose freedom, so they are its antithesis. Symbol or foundation would suggest they support freedom.
items.clue: claimed to defend freedom, yet

items.prompt: "Antithesis" combines "anti-" (against) and "thesis" (a position or idea). What does that suggest?

options.text: an idea that has been proven true
an idea that supports another idea
an idea set directly against another
an idea that comes before another

items.hint: Think about what "anti-" means in words like "antibiotic" or "antisocial."
items.explanation: Anti- means against. An antithesis is a position set against another one: its opposite.

items.prompt: Which sentence uses antithesis as a rhetorical device?

options.text: "The sky was a deep, glowing orange."
"Please remember to bring your library book tomorrow."
"We walked to the park and played on the swings."
"Ask not what your country can do for you; ask what you can do for your country."

items.hint: Look for opposite ideas set side by side in a balanced sentence.
items.explanation: The famous line places two opposite ideas in balanced form, "what your country can do for you" against "what you can do for your country." That is antithesis.

items.prompt: Is the second item the antithesis of the first?
items.passage: First: a chef who carefully measures every ingredient. Second: a chef who measures most ingredients but sometimes estimates the salt.
items.hint: Are these two chefs complete opposites?
items.explanation: No. The second chef is only slightly different. The antithesis of a careful measurer would be someone who never measures at all.

words.definition: gentle and harmless; in medicine, not dangerous or cancerous

hero.text: The glowing creature looked frightening, but Kai realized it was benign: it only wanted the scraps of fruit in his bag.

words.everyday: The doctor reassured Grandpa that the lump on his arm was benign and would not spread.

contrast.nonExample: The storm grew stronger and knocked out power across three towns.
contrast.explanation: A destructive storm causes harm. Benign describes something harmless or kindly.

items.prompt: What does "benign" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: Most bacteria living in the human gut are benign, and many even help us digest food.
items.hint: Many of them "even help us." What does that suggest?
items.explanation: Benign means harmless. Gut bacteria that do no damage, and even help, are benign.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: Although the software update looked suspicious, the security team confirmed it was ___ and contained no hidden programs that could damage the network.

wrong.a: Malicious is the opposite: designed to cause harm.
wrong.c: Outdated means old; age is not the issue.
wrong.d: Encrypted means coded for privacy, which says nothing about harm.

items.hint: "No hidden programs that could damage" tells you it is safe.
items.explanation: Software that contains nothing harmful is benign. Malicious means intended to harm, the opposite.
items.clue: contained no hidden programs that could damage

items.prompt: Which word means the OPPOSITE of "benign" in this sentence?
items.passage: The biopsy showed that the growth was benign.
items.hint: In medicine, what is the dangerous opposite of a benign growth?
items.explanation: In medicine, benign means not cancerous, and malignant means cancerous and dangerous. Mild and minor are closer to benign.

items.prompt: Which word best describes the grandmother's expression?
items.passage: The grandmother watched the toddlers knock over her flowerpots with a benign smile, as if nothing could possibly upset her.
items.hint: She is gentle and untroubled.
items.explanation: A benign smile is kindly and gentle, with no hostility. Stern or sarcastic would suggest disapproval, which the passage rules out.

items.prompt: Is the situation described benign?
items.passage: A new invasive beetle has spread through the forest, killing thousands of ash trees in just five years.
items.hint: Is the beetle harmless?
items.explanation: No. A beetle killing thousands of trees is harmful, the opposite of benign.

words.definition: changing mood or behavior suddenly and without a clear reason

hero.text: The capricious wind kept shifting direction, so Nova had to adjust her flight path every few seconds.

words.everyday: Mountain weather is capricious: a sunny morning can turn into a hailstorm by noon.

contrast.nonExample: Every evening at exactly six, the lighthouse beam begins its slow, steady sweep.
contrast.explanation: The lighthouse is completely regular and predictable. Capricious describes sudden, unpredictable changes.

items.prompt: What does "capricious" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: The ruler was so capricious that he might reward a servant one day and banish him the next for the very same action.
items.hint: Same action, opposite results on different days.
items.explanation: Capricious means changing suddenly for no clear reason. Rewarding and then punishing the same behavior shows unpredictable whims.

items.prompt: Is this person capricious?
items.passage: Ms. Alvarez posts her grading rubric at the start of the year and applies it the same way to every assignment.
items.hint: Is her behavior unpredictable?
items.explanation: No. Ms. Alvarez is consistent and predictable, the opposite of capricious.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: Investors grew nervous about the ___ market, where stock prices soared on Monday, crashed on Tuesday, and recovered by Wednesday for no obvious reason.

wrong.c: Stagnant means not changing, the opposite of these wild swings.
wrong.a: Generous does not describe price movements.
wrong.b: Transparent means easy to see through or understand, which this market is not.

items.hint: Big, sudden swings "for no obvious reason."
items.explanation: Sudden ups and downs "for no obvious reason" make the market capricious. Stagnant would mean not moving at all.
items.clue: soared; crashed; recovered; for no obvious reason

items.prompt: Which word best describes the cat's behavior?
items.passage: One minute the cat purred on Leo's lap; the next, with no warning and nothing having changed, it swatted his hand and stalked away.
items.hint: The key is the sudden, unexplained change.
items.explanation: Capricious fits because the cat's mood flips suddenly "with no warning and nothing having changed." Hostile would suggest steady unfriendliness, not a sudden switch.

items.prompt: Which word means the OPPOSITE of "capricious" in this sentence?
items.passage: Fans complained about the referee's capricious calls, which seemed to change from one play to the next.
items.hint: Look for a word meaning "the same every time."
items.explanation: Capricious means unpredictable. Consistent means applied the same way every time, the opposite. Erratic and impulsive are close to capricious.

words.definition: to find a way around a rule, obstacle, or problem, often cleverly

hero.text: When the main bridge was blocked, Pixel circumvented the traffic jam by guiding everyone through an old service tunnel.

words.everyday: Engineers designed a bypass canal to circumvent the dangerous rapids on the river.

contrast.nonExample: Lena waited patiently in the long line and paid the full entry fee.
contrast.explanation: Lena goes straight through the normal process. Circumventing means getting around a rule or obstacle instead.

items.prompt: "Circumvent" comes from "circum-" (around) and "vent" (come or go). What does it most likely mean?
items.hint: "Circum-" appears in "circumference," the distance around a circle.
items.explanation: Circum- means around and vent means go, so circumvent means to go around an obstacle or rule.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: Some students tried to ___ the school's website filter by using a proxy server, which disguised the blocked sites as approved ones.
items.hint: They are trying to get around the filter.
items.explanation: Using a disguise to get past the filter is circumventing it: finding a way around a rule instead of obeying it.
items.clue: disguised the blocked sites as approved ones

items.prompt: Which action circumvents a rule?

options.text: A company openly pays the new tax on time.
A company moves its address to another country to avoid paying a new tax.
A company protests the new tax at city hall.
A company pays extra tax by mistake.

wrong.a: Paying the tax follows the rule.
wrong.c: Protesting challenges the rule openly; it does not get around it.
wrong.d: Paying by mistake is an error, not a way around a rule.

items.hint: Look for a clever way around the rule, not obeying or protesting it.
items.explanation: Moving its address to dodge the tax is circumventing: the company avoids the rule without breaking or challenging it directly.

items.prompt: Which word best describes what the river did?
items.passage: When a fallen boulder blocked its path, the stream slowly carved a new channel around the rock and continued downhill.
items.hint: The stream found a way around, not through.
items.explanation: The stream went around the boulder rather than removing it: it circumvented the obstacle. Destroyed would mean it broke the rock apart.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what circumvent means.

chunks.text: To circumvent the long security line,
the travelers
used the express lane their airline membership allowed.
waited in it for three full hours.

items.hint: Circumventing means finding a way around.
items.explanation: Using the express lane is a way around the long line. Waiting in it for hours is going through it, not around it.

words.definition: clear, logical, and convincing

hero.text: Rex presented such a cogent plan, with evidence for every step, that the whole team agreed in minutes.

words.everyday: The debate judges praised Aisha's cogent closing argument, which tied every point back to the evidence.

contrast.nonExample: Nate's speech was loud and passionate, but he jumped between unrelated points and never gave a reason.
contrast.explanation: Passion is not the same as cogency. A cogent argument is logical and convincing, whatever its volume.

items.prompt: What does "cogent" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: The lawyer's cogent argument, supported by clear evidence and careful reasoning, persuaded the jury.
items.hint: It is "supported by clear evidence and careful reasoning" and it "persuaded."
items.explanation: Cogent means clear, logical, and convincing. The argument persuaded the jury through evidence and reasoning.

items.prompt: Which word best describes Ming's essay, according to the teacher?
items.passage: "Your essay is short," the teacher wrote, "but every paragraph builds logically on the last, and your evidence leaves little room for doubt."

wrong.d: Verbose means wordy; the essay is short.
wrong.b: Ambiguous means unclear; this essay leaves little doubt.
wrong.c: Elaborate suggests lots of detail and length.

items.hint: Short, logical, and hard to doubt.
items.explanation: Cogent fits: logical structure and convincing evidence. Verbose and elaborate suggest length, which the teacher says it lacks.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: Scientists rejected the theory because it rested on a single study, but the new paper's case, built on twenty years of data from five continents, was far more ___.
items.hint: Compare a single study with twenty years of worldwide data.
items.explanation: A case built on twenty years of global data is strong and convincing: cogent. Flimsy describes the earlier single-study theory.
items.clue: twenty years of data from five continents

items.prompt: Which word is closest in meaning to "cogent" in this sentence?
items.passage: She offered a cogent explanation for why the bridge had failed.
items.hint: Which word means convincing?
items.explanation: Compelling means convincing in a way that demands attention, like cogent. Lengthy and complicated describe size and difficulty, not persuasiveness.

items.prompt: Which speaker uses "cogent" correctly?

options.text: "He gave a cogent yawn during the movie."
"The puppy is cogent and loves to play fetch."
"The soup was so cogent that I asked for seconds."
"Her cogent reasoning convinced even the people who disagreed at first."

items.hint: Cogent describes arguments or reasoning.
items.explanation: Cogent describes clear, convincing reasoning, so it fits "reasoning convinced even the people who disagreed." It does not describe food, yawns, or pets.

words.definition: happening or existing at the same time

hero.text: Bolt had to handle two concurrent emergencies: a flooded subway and a stuck elevator, both starting at noon.

words.everyday: The museum is running two concurrent exhibits, one on ancient Egypt and one on modern photography.

contrast.nonExample: First the band played the anthem, and afterward the game began.
contrast.explanation: These events happen one after another. Concurrent events happen at the same time.

items.prompt: What does "concurrent" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: The judge ordered the two sentences to be concurrent, so the prisoner would serve both at the same time rather than one after the other.

options.text: taking place at the same time

items.hint: "At the same time rather than one after the other."
items.explanation: Concurrent means happening at the same time. The passage defines it directly: both sentences run together.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: Historians note that the Renaissance in Italy was roughly ___ with the rise of powerful trading cities like Venice and Florence, which funded many of its artists.
items.hint: The two developments happened in the same period.
items.explanation: The Renaissance and the rise of trading cities overlapped in time, so they were concurrent. Previous would mean one came before the other.
items.clue: roughly; with the rise of

items.prompt: Are these events concurrent?
items.passage: Jada finished her piano lesson at 4:00, then walked to soccer practice, which started at 4:30.
items.hint: Did the events overlap in time?
items.explanation: No. The lesson ended before practice began, so the events were consecutive, not concurrent.

items.prompt: Which word means the OPPOSITE of "concurrent" in this sentence?
items.passage: The computer can run several concurrent tasks without slowing down.
items.hint: Find the word meaning "one after another."
items.explanation: Concurrent means at the same time. Sequential means one after another, the opposite. Simultaneous is a synonym.

items.prompt: "Concurrent" comes from "con-" (together) and "cur" (run, as in "current"). How do those parts explain the word?
items.hint: Things that "run together" share the same time.
items.explanation: Con- means together and cur means run, so concurrent events run together, happening at the same time.

words.definition: to accept or allow behavior that is considered wrong, as if it were acceptable

hero.text: Kai made it clear he would never condone using powers to scare civilians, even as a prank.

words.everyday: The school handbook states that the district does not condone cyberbullying of any kind.

contrast.nonExample: Mr. Diaz stopped the game immediately when he saw a student cheating.
contrast.explanation: Mr. Diaz does not allow the wrong behavior. Condoning means letting it pass as though it were acceptable.

items.prompt: Is this person condoning the behavior?
items.passage: When his older son lied about finishing his chores, the father smiled and said, "That's okay, everyone stretches the truth sometimes."
items.hint: Does the father treat the lie as acceptable?
items.explanation: Yes. By treating the lie as fine, the father condones it: he accepts wrong behavior as if it were acceptable.

items.prompt: Which word best describes the coach's response?
items.passage: Several players shoved opponents after the whistle. The coach saw it but said nothing and did not bench anyone.

wrong.a: He benched no one, so he did not punish.
wrong.b: Celebrating would mean praising it openly; he simply let it go.
wrong.c: The shoving already happened; he did nothing to stop it.

items.hint: Silence and no consequences send a message.
items.explanation: By ignoring the shoving with no consequences, the coach condoned it. Celebrated would mean openly praising it, which goes further than the passage shows.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: Although the senator admired the protesters' goals, she said she could not ___ their decision to damage public property.
items.hint: "Although" signals a contrast between the goals and the actions.
items.explanation: She supports the goals but refuses to accept the wrong action, so she cannot condone it. Admire would contradict the contrast set up by "although."
items.clue: Although; admired the goals; damage public property

items.prompt: Which word means the OPPOSITE of "condone" in this sentence?
items.passage: The company says it does not condone unsafe working conditions in its factories.
items.hint: Which word means "strongly disapprove of"?
items.explanation: Condone means accept wrong behavior. Condemn means openly declare it wrong, the opposite. The other three are close to condone.

items.prompt: Which speaker uses "condone" correctly?

options.text: "She condoned the trophy to the winning team."
"The teacher condoned us a great story yesterday."
"I condone this pizza; it's the best in town."
"Leaving trash at the campsite isn't okay, and I won't condone it."

items.hint: Condone means accept or excuse wrong behavior.
items.explanation: Refusing to condone littering means refusing to treat it as acceptable. The other lines confuse condone with praising, giving, or telling.

words.definition: to confirm a statement or idea by providing additional, independent evidence

hero.text: Juniper's security camera footage corroborated Nova's account of when the power went out.

words.everyday: Two other astronomers corroborated the discovery by observing the same comet from different observatories.

contrast.nonExample: The suspect insisted three times that he had been home all evening.
contrast.explanation: Repeating your own story is not corroboration. Corroboration comes from a separate source that confirms it.

items.prompt: What does "corroborated" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: The diary entries corroborated the soldier's letters: both described the same battle on the same day.
items.hint: Two separate sources tell the same story.
items.explanation: Corroborate means to confirm with additional, independent evidence. The diary and the letters are separate sources that agree.

items.prompt: Which word best describes what the second lab did?
items.passage: A lab in Japan reported a new material that conducts electricity perfectly. Months later, a lab in Brazil repeated the experiment independently and got the same result.

wrong.a: The Brazilian lab did not invent it; it repeated the experiment.
wrong.b: Disputing would mean disagreeing; they got the same result.
wrong.c: Advertising is promoting, not confirming.

items.hint: A separate group confirms the original finding.
items.explanation: An independent lab getting the same result corroborates the finding. Disputed would mean it challenged the result.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: The historian was skeptical of the legend until archaeologists uncovered coins and pottery that ___ the story of a busy trading port at the site.
items.hint: The new finds support a story she doubted.
items.explanation: The coins and pottery are separate physical evidence that confirm the legend, so they corroborated it.
items.clue: was skeptical until; uncovered coins and pottery

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what corroborate means.

chunks.text: A second witness
corroborated Maria's report
by describing the same blue car at the same corner.
by insisting she had seen a red truck somewhere else.

items.hint: Corroborating evidence agrees with the original account.
items.explanation: Describing the same car at the same place confirms Maria's report. A different vehicle in a different place would contradict it.

items.prompt: Does the new evidence corroborate the claim?
items.passage: A company claims its battery lasts ten hours. Independent testers find it dies after four.
items.hint: Does the testers' result agree with the claim?
items.explanation: No. The testers' results contradict the claim. Corroborating evidence would show the battery really does last about ten hours.

words.definition: a sharp division or contrast between two opposite things or groups

hero.text: Rex rejected the dichotomy of "heroes versus villains," arguing that most people are somewhere in between.

words.everyday: The essay explores the dichotomy between city life and country life in nineteenth-century novels.

contrast.nonExample: The class discussed many shades of opinion about the new schedule, from strongly for to mildly against.
contrast.explanation: A wide range of views is not a dichotomy. A dichotomy splits things into two sharply opposed parts.

items.prompt: What does "dichotomy" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: The speech set up a dichotomy between "the people" and "the elites," as if everyone belonged to exactly one of the two groups.

options.text: a sharp division into two opposing parts

items.hint: Everyone belongs to "exactly one of the two groups."
items.explanation: A dichotomy splits something into two sharply opposed parts. The speech divides everyone into two groups.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: Many scientists now reject the old ___ between "nature" and "nurture," arguing that genes and environment work together rather than as rivals.

wrong.c: An alliance means a partnership, the opposite of rivals.
wrong.a: An experiment is a test, not a division of ideas.
wrong.b: Tradition is close, but the passage stresses the split into two rival sides.

items.hint: The old view set two things against each other as rivals.
items.explanation: Treating nature and nurture as rivals is a dichotomy: a sharp two-way split. Scientists now see them as working together.
items.clue: between "nature" and "nurture"; rather than as rivals

items.prompt: "Dichotomy" comes from Greek parts meaning "in two" and "cutting." What does that suggest?

options.text: cutting something into two opposed parts

items.hint: Put the parts together: "cutting in two."
items.explanation: A dichotomy literally "cuts in two," dividing an idea or group into two contrasting halves.

items.prompt: Which word best names what the author criticizes?
items.passage: The author argues that the choice between "art" and "science" is false: architects, game designers, and medical illustrators all combine both every day.

wrong.b: A paradox seems self-contradictory but may be true; here the issue is an either-or split.
wrong.c: A hypothesis is a testable idea.
wrong.d: A compromise blends two sides, which is what the author recommends, not criticizes.

items.hint: The author rejects splitting things into two opposite camps.
items.explanation: Splitting work into "art" versus "science" is a dichotomy, which the author calls false. A paradox is a statement that seems to contradict itself, which is a different idea.

items.prompt: Does this describe a dichotomy?
items.passage: In the novel, the two kingdoms are complete opposites: one values only order and obedience, the other only freedom and chaos.
items.hint: Are there two sharply opposed sides?
items.explanation: Yes. Two kingdoms defined as complete opposites form a dichotomy: a sharp division into two contrasting parts.

words.definition: intended to teach, especially a moral lesson, sometimes in a preachy way

hero.text: Pixel's safety video was so didactic, with a lesson every ten seconds, that the younger heroes started rolling their eyes.

words.everyday: Aesop's fables are didactic: each short story ends with a clear moral, such as "slow and steady wins the race."

contrast.nonExample: The comedy show was pure entertainment, with no message beyond making the audience laugh.
contrast.explanation: A work made only to entertain is not didactic. Didactic works are meant to instruct.

items.prompt: What does "didactic" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: The children's book was openly didactic, ending each chapter with a list of lessons about honesty and sharing.
items.hint: Each chapter ends with "a list of lessons."
items.explanation: Didactic means intended to teach, especially morals. The lessons at the end of each chapter make the book didactic.

items.prompt: Which word best describes the critic's complaint?
items.passage: "The film has a good message about protecting oceans," the critic wrote, "but the characters keep stopping to lecture the audience, and the story suffers for it."

wrong.a: Subtle means delicate and understated; lecturing is anything but.
wrong.c: Suspenseful describes tension, not lecturing.
wrong.d: Satire uses humor or irony to criticize; this film simply preaches.

items.hint: Characters "keep stopping to lecture."
items.explanation: Constant lecturing makes the film didactic in a preachy way. Subtle is the opposite, and satirical would mean using humor to criticize.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: Medieval morality plays were deeply ___: characters with names like Greed and Good Deeds acted out lessons about how audiences should live.
items.hint: The plays existed to teach audiences how to live.
items.explanation: Plays designed to teach moral lessons are didactic. Characters named after virtues and vices make the teaching purpose obvious.
items.clue: acted out lessons about how audiences should live

items.prompt: Is this work didactic?
items.passage: A song describes the feeling of a summer evening, with no message, advice, or lesson, just images of fireflies and warm air.
items.hint: Is the song trying to teach anything?
items.explanation: No. The song simply captures a mood. A didactic work would try to instruct or deliver a lesson.

items.prompt: Which speaker uses "didactic" correctly?

options.text: "I felt didactic after running five miles."
"Our cat is didactic; she sleeps all afternoon."
"That thunderstorm was really didactic last night."
"The museum guide was a bit didactic, turning every painting into a lecture about good behavior."

items.hint: Didactic describes teaching or lecturing.
items.explanation: A guide who turns everything into a moral lecture is didactic. The other lines use the word for tiredness, sleepiness, or weather.

words.definition: to spread information or ideas widely

hero.text: Bolt helped disseminate the evacuation warning, broadcasting it on every radio channel in the city.

words.everyday: The printing press allowed reformers to disseminate their ideas across Europe in months rather than decades.

contrast.nonExample: Jo whispered the secret to her best friend and made her promise not to tell anyone.
contrast.explanation: Telling one person and keeping it secret is the opposite of disseminating. Disseminating spreads information widely.

items.prompt: What does "disseminate" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: Health officials used posters, radio ads, and social media to disseminate information about the vaccine to every neighborhood.
items.hint: Posters, radio, and social media, reaching "every neighborhood."
items.explanation: Disseminate means spread widely. Using many channels to reach every neighborhood is disseminating information.

items.prompt: "Disseminate" comes from Latin words for "apart" and "seed." Which picture best matches the word?

options.text: a farmer locking seeds in a shed
a farmer scattering seeds across a field

items.hint: Seeds scattered "apart" in many directions.
items.explanation: Disseminate originally meant scattering seed. Today it means scattering ideas or information widely.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: During the Revolutionary War, colonists used pamphlets and newspapers to ___ arguments for independence to farmers and merchants throughout the thirteen colonies.

wrong.b: Suppressing means preventing spread, the opposite.
wrong.c: The colonists already shared a language; translating is not the point.
wrong.d: Memorizing keeps ideas in one head rather than spreading them.

items.hint: Pamphlets carried the arguments far and wide.
items.explanation: Spreading arguments "throughout the thirteen colonies" with pamphlets is disseminating them. Suppress would mean stopping their spread.
items.clue: pamphlets and newspapers; throughout the thirteen colonies

items.prompt: Which word is closest in meaning to "disseminated" in this sentence?
items.passage: The researchers disseminated their findings at conferences around the world.
items.hint: Which word means "passed around widely"?
items.explanation: Circulated means passed around widely, matching disseminated. Concealed is the opposite.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what disseminate means.

chunks.text: The student newspaper
disseminated the survey results
to every classroom and the school website.
to one teacher, who locked them in a drawer.

items.hint: Disseminating spreads information widely.
items.explanation: Sending results to every classroom and online spreads them widely. Giving them to one person who hides them is the opposite.

words.definition: insisting that your beliefs are completely right, without considering evidence or other views

hero.text: Bolt was dogmatic about his training method, refusing to even look at Juniper's data showing a better way.

words.everyday: The new club president was so dogmatic about the rules that he would not discuss any suggestion for change.

contrast.nonExample: After hearing the new evidence, Dr. Lee said, "I may have been wrong; let's test it again."
contrast.explanation: Dr. Lee is open to changing her mind. A dogmatic person refuses to consider other evidence or views.

items.prompt: Which person is dogmatic?

options.text: Ari changes his opinion after reading a convincing article.
Sana insists her view is right and refuses to look at any evidence against it.
Felix admits he isn't sure and asks for more information.
Mei listens carefully to both sides before deciding.

items.hint: Look for someone who refuses to consider other views.
items.explanation: Sana insists she is right and refuses to look at evidence, which is dogmatic. The others are open-minded.

items.prompt: Which word best describes the professor?
items.passage: For thirty years, the professor taught that the theory was beyond question. When students raised new research that challenged it, he dismissed them without reading a single page.

wrong.b: Confidence alone does not mean refusing to look at evidence.
wrong.d: Experience is true of him but does not explain refusing to read.
wrong.a: A skeptic questions claims; he never questions his own view.

items.hint: He refuses to even read the evidence.
items.explanation: Dismissing new research without reading it shows he treats his view as beyond question: dogmatic. Confident people can still consider evidence. Skeptical means doubting, but he doubts only the new ideas, never his own.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: Galileo's critics were ___ in their belief that the sun circled the Earth; some reportedly refused even to look through his telescope.
items.hint: They refused to look at evidence.
items.explanation: Refusing to look at evidence that might challenge a belief is dogmatic. Curious people would have looked.
items.clue: refused even to look through his telescope

items.prompt: Which word means the OPPOSITE of "dogmatic" in this sentence?
items.passage: Good scientists try not to be dogmatic about their theories.
items.hint: Look for a word meaning "willing to consider new ideas."
items.explanation: Dogmatic means refusing to consider other views. Open-minded is the opposite. Rigid, stubborn, and opinionated are all close to dogmatic.

items.prompt: Which line sounds the most dogmatic?

options.text: "I think this plan could work, but I'd like to hear other ideas."
"There is only one correct way to do this, and there's nothing to discuss."
"Let's look at the data before we decide."
"You might be right; I hadn't thought of that."

items.hint: Find the speaker who shuts down discussion.
items.explanation: Insisting there is "only one correct way" and "nothing to discuss" is dogmatic. The other lines show openness to evidence and other views.

words.definition: lasting for only a very short time

hero.text: Kai's ice sculpture of the team was ephemeral: by noon, the summer sun had melted it into a puddle.

words.everyday: Mayflies are famous for their ephemeral adult lives, which often last only a single day.

contrast.nonExample: The ancient pyramids of Giza have stood for more than four thousand years.
contrast.explanation: Something that lasts thousands of years is enduring, the opposite of ephemeral.

items.prompt: What does "ephemeral" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: The rainbow was ephemeral, fading from the sky just seconds after we noticed it.
items.hint: It faded "just seconds after."
items.explanation: Ephemeral means lasting only a short time. The rainbow disappeared within seconds.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: Many internet trends are ___: a dance or meme can dominate every feed for a week and then vanish so completely that no one remembers it a month later.
items.hint: Popular for a week, forgotten in a month.
items.explanation: Trends that "vanish" after a week are ephemeral, lasting only briefly. Permanent is the opposite.
items.clue: for a week and then vanish

items.prompt: Which word best fits the artist's work?
items.passage: The artist draws huge chalk murals on city sidewalks, knowing the next rainstorm will wash them away completely.
items.hint: What will the rain do to the art?
items.explanation: Art designed to be washed away by the next rain is ephemeral: it lasts only a short time. Abstract describes style, not duration.

items.prompt: Which word means the OPPOSITE of "ephemeral" in this sentence?
items.passage: The poet compares fame to a soap bubble: shining, admired, and ephemeral.

wrong.c: Fleeting is a synonym, not an opposite.
wrong.a: Fragile means easily broken, which is related but not the opposite.
wrong.b: Delicate describes how easily something is damaged, not how long it lasts.

items.hint: Find the word meaning "lasting a long time."
items.explanation: Ephemeral means short-lived. Enduring means lasting a long time, the opposite. Fleeting is a synonym, and fragile and delicate describe breakability rather than duration.

items.prompt: Is this ephemeral?
items.passage: A family passes down the same handmade quilt for six generations, and it is still used every winter.
items.hint: Did the quilt last a short time?
items.explanation: No. Lasting six generations makes the quilt enduring, the opposite of ephemeral.

words.definition: to make a problem, pain, or bad situation worse

hero.text: Rex's angry shouting only exacerbated the panic in the crowd, so Nova stepped in with a calm voice.

words.everyday: Scratching a mosquito bite usually exacerbates the itching instead of relieving it.

contrast.nonExample: Putting ice on the sprained ankle reduced the swelling within an hour.
contrast.explanation: The ice made the problem better. Exacerbating means making a problem worse.

items.prompt: What does "exacerbated" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: The long drought exacerbated the food shortage, leaving even fewer crops to harvest.
items.hint: There were "even fewer crops" afterward.
items.explanation: Exacerbate means make worse. The drought deepened a shortage that already existed.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: Cutting down the mangrove forests along the coast ___ the damage from storms, because the trees had once absorbed much of the waves' force.

wrong.c: Prevented would mean the damage stopped, but losing the trees removed protection.
wrong.d: Measuring describes studying damage, not changing it.
wrong.a: Reversing would mean undoing damage.

items.hint: Without the trees, are the storms' effects better or worse?
items.explanation: Removing trees that had absorbed wave energy made storm damage worse, so cutting them exacerbated the damage.
items.clue: had once absorbed much of the waves' force

items.prompt: Which word best describes the effect of the apology?
items.passage: The two friends had a small disagreement. Then one posted a sarcastic "apology" online for the whole class to see, and the argument grew into a feud that lasted months.

wrong.c: Resolving would end the conflict; it grew instead.
wrong.a: The disagreement existed before the post, so the post did not cause it.
wrong.b: The post engaged with the argument publicly rather than ignoring it.

items.hint: The disagreement already existed. What did the post do to it?
items.explanation: The disagreement already existed; the post made it much worse, so it exacerbated the conflict. Caused would mean it started the conflict, which it did not.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what exacerbate means.

chunks.text: Staying up late every night
exacerbated Owen's headaches,
which grew stronger and more frequent.
which finally faded away completely.

items.hint: Exacerbating makes a problem worse.
items.explanation: Headaches that grow "stronger and more frequent" have been exacerbated. Fading away would mean the problem improved.

items.prompt: Which word means the OPPOSITE of "exacerbate" in this sentence?
items.passage: Economists warned that raising prices again would only exacerbate the crisis.
items.hint: Which word means "make less severe"?
items.explanation: Exacerbate means make worse. Alleviate means make less severe, the opposite. Aggravate and intensify are synonyms, and prolong means make it last longer.

words.definition: to use known facts or trends to estimate or predict what is unknown

hero.text: Using the storm's speed over the last hour, Pixel extrapolated that it would reach the harbor by midnight.

words.everyday: From ten years of temperature records, the scientists extrapolated how warm the lake might be by 2050.

contrast.nonExample: Mia measured the plant's height every morning and wrote down exactly what she saw.
contrast.explanation: Recording what you observe is not extrapolating. Extrapolating goes beyond the data to predict the unknown.

items.prompt: What does "extrapolate" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: Since the town's population grew by 500 people every year for a decade, planners extrapolated that it would reach 20,000 within six years.

options.text: to predict using a known trend
to count every person by hand

wrong.c: Counting is direct measurement, not prediction.
wrong.d: Extrapolation uses information; it is not a blind guess.
wrong.a: Nothing in the sentence is about arguing.

items.hint: They used past growth to predict future size.
items.explanation: Extrapolating means extending a known pattern to estimate the unknown. The planners used ten years of growth to predict the future.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: The researchers studied only 200 students, so they warned readers not to ___ their results to every teenager in the country.
items.hint: Stretching a small sample to a whole country.
items.explanation: Applying results from 200 students to all teenagers would extrapolate beyond the data, which the researchers warn against.
items.clue: studied only 200 students; to every teenager in the country

items.prompt: Which word best describes what Ravi did?
items.passage: Ravi noticed his phone battery lost 10% every hour. At 40% and noon, he concluded it would die around 4 p.m.

wrong.a: Exaggerating means overstating; his estimate follows the data.
wrong.b: He did not charge the phone.
wrong.c: He observed the drain first, but the prediction is extrapolation.

items.hint: He used a pattern to predict a future time.
items.explanation: Ravi extended the pattern (10% per hour) to predict when the battery would die. That is extrapolating. Observing describes noticing the pattern, but the prediction goes further.

items.prompt: "Extrapolate" begins with "extra-," meaning "outside" or "beyond." How does this help explain the word?

options.text: reaching conclusions beyond the data you have

items.hint: "Extra-" as in "extraordinary": beyond the ordinary.
items.explanation: Extra- means beyond. Extrapolating takes a known pattern beyond the existing data to predict something new.

items.prompt: Is this an example of extrapolating?
items.passage: After reading the first three chapters, in which the detective solves each case by noticing small details, Leila predicts the final mystery will be solved the same way.
items.hint: Does Leila use a pattern to predict something unknown?
items.explanation: Yes. Leila extends a pattern from the chapters she has read to predict the ending she has not read. That is extrapolating.

words.definition: to make a process or action easier or help it happen

hero.text: Juniper built a ramp to facilitate the evacuation, so people with wheelchairs and strollers could leave quickly.

words.everyday: The teacher facilitated the class discussion by asking questions and making sure everyone had a turn to speak.

contrast.nonExample: The broken elevator made it harder for visitors to reach the top floor.
contrast.explanation: The broken elevator made things harder. Facilitating makes a process easier.

items.prompt: What does "facilitate" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: The new translation app helps facilitate conversations between doctors and patients who speak different languages.
items.hint: What does the app do for the conversations?
items.explanation: Facilitate means make easier or help happen. The app helps people who speak different languages understand each other.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: The Erie Canal, completed in 1825, greatly ___ trade between the Atlantic coast and the Midwest by cutting shipping costs by about 90 percent.
items.hint: Cheaper shipping makes trade easier.
items.explanation: Cutting costs made trade much easier, so the canal facilitated it. Discouraged and delayed would mean it made trade harder.
items.clue: cutting shipping costs by about 90 percent

items.prompt: Which word means the OPPOSITE of "facilitate" in this sentence?
items.passage: Clear signs facilitate the flow of visitors through the museum.
items.hint: Which word means "make harder"?
items.explanation: Facilitate means make easier. Hinder means make harder, the opposite. Ease, guide, and speed are close to facilitate.

items.prompt: Which word best describes Ms. Kim's role?
items.passage: Ms. Kim does not tell the debate club what to think. She sets the schedule, keeps time, and makes sure every member gets a fair chance to speak.

wrong.b: Dictating means controlling or ordering, which she avoids.
wrong.d: She organizes; she does not compete.
wrong.a: Nothing shows her criticizing members.

items.hint: She makes the process run smoothly without controlling the content.
items.explanation: Ms. Kim makes the club's discussions run smoothly: she facilitates. Dictating would mean telling them what to think, which the passage rules out.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what facilitate means.

chunks.text: To facilitate group projects,
the library
added large tables and whiteboards in the study rooms.
removed all the tables and banned talking.

items.hint: Facilitating makes something easier.
items.explanation: Tables and whiteboards make group work easier, so they facilitate it. Removing tables and banning talking would hinder group work.

words.definition: a force or reason that causes something to start or move forward faster

hero.text: The near-disaster at the dam gave the team the impetus to build a real early-warning system.

words.everyday: The 1957 launch of Sputnik gave the United States the impetus to invest heavily in science education.

contrast.nonExample: The class finished the mural on schedule, exactly as planned months earlier.
contrast.explanation: Nothing pushed the project forward or started it here. An impetus is the driving force behind a change or action.

items.prompt: What does "impetus" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: Her grandmother's illness was the impetus for Dana's decision to study medicine.

options.text: a reason that pushes something to happen

items.hint: What pushed Dana to make her decision?
items.explanation: An impetus is a force or reason that drives an action. The illness motivated Dana to study medicine.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: The deadly factory fire of 1911 provided the ___ for new workplace safety laws in New York, which lawmakers had ignored for years.

wrong.c: An obstacle blocks change; the fire caused it.
wrong.d: A summary describes events; it does not drive them.
wrong.a: An audience watches; it is not a cause.

items.hint: Laws ignored for years suddenly passed. What did the fire provide?
items.explanation: The fire pushed lawmakers to finally act, so it was the impetus for the laws. An obstacle would have stopped them.
items.clue: had ignored for years

items.prompt: Which word best describes the role of the viral video?
items.passage: For months, the neighborhood's petition for a crosswalk got little attention. Then a video of a near-accident spread online, and within weeks the city painted the crosswalk.

wrong.d: An obstacle would slow the project; the video sped it up.
wrong.a: The crosswalk is the consequence; the video came first and caused it.
wrong.b: A compromise is a deal between two sides.

items.hint: The video got things moving.
items.explanation: The video drove the city to act quickly, so it was the impetus. The crosswalk is the consequence, not the video.

items.prompt: Does this describe an impetus?
items.passage: After failing his driving test, Tomás practiced parallel parking every day for a month.
items.hint: Did something push Tomás into action?
items.explanation: Yes. Failing the test was the impetus that drove Tomás to practice every day.

items.prompt: Which word is closest in meaning to "impetus" in this sentence?
items.passage: The discovery of gold in 1848 was the impetus for a huge wave of migration to California.
items.hint: Which word means "something that causes change to happen"?
items.explanation: A catalyst triggers or speeds up change, very close to impetus. A barrier would block migration.

words.definition: strange or out of place because it does not fit with its surroundings

hero.text: Bolt's bright party hat looked incongruous at the serious council meeting.

words.everyday: A modern glass skyscraper looked incongruous among the village's centuries-old stone cottages.

contrast.nonExample: At the beach party, everyone wore swimsuits and sandals.
contrast.explanation: The clothing matches the setting. Incongruous describes something that clashes with or does not fit its surroundings.

items.prompt: What does "incongruous" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: His cheerful whistling seemed incongruous at the quiet, solemn memorial service.
items.hint: Does cheerful whistling fit a solemn service?
items.explanation: Incongruous means out of place. Cheerful whistling clashes with a solemn setting.

items.prompt: "Incongruous" combines "in-" (not) with "congruous" (fitting together). What does the word mean?
items.hint: In math, congruent shapes match exactly.
items.explanation: In- means not, and congruous means fitting together, so incongruous means not fitting, out of place.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: The director chose a cheerful pop song for the film's saddest scene; the ___ music made some viewers uncomfortable and others think more deeply.
items.hint: Cheerful music in a sad scene creates a clash.
items.explanation: Cheerful music does not fit a sad scene, so it is incongruous. Fitting would mean it matched, which contradicts the clash.
items.clue: cheerful pop song for the saddest scene

items.prompt: Which word best describes the speaker's remark?
items.passage: In the middle of a serious debate about climate policy, one candidate suddenly began talking about his favorite pizza toppings.
items.hint: The remark does not fit the serious topic.
items.explanation: Pizza toppings during a serious policy debate are out of place, so the remark is incongruous. It is not hostile, and it certainly is not persuasive.

items.prompt: Is anything incongruous here?
items.passage: In a quiet library reading room, students sit at wooden tables, turning pages and taking notes.
items.hint: Does anything clash with the setting?
items.explanation: No. Everything fits the library setting. Something incongruous would clash, like a blaring radio.

words.definition: to place two things side by side, especially to highlight their differences

hero.text: Pixel's exhibit juxtaposed photos of the river before and after the cleanup, so visitors could see the change instantly.

words.everyday: The photographer juxtaposed a luxury hotel with the crowded tents beside it to show the gap between rich and poor.

contrast.nonExample: The museum displayed the paintings in separate rooms on different floors.
contrast.explanation: Placing things far apart does not invite direct comparison. Juxtaposing means placing them side by side.

items.prompt: What does "juxtaposes" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: The poem juxtaposes images of a busy, noisy city with images of a silent forest.

options.text: places side by side for contrast

items.hint: Two very different images appear together.
items.explanation: Juxtapose means to place two things side by side, often to show contrast. The poem pairs the noisy city with the silent forest.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: In her speech, the activist ___ the company's record profits with its workers' falling wages, letting the contrast make her argument for her.

wrong.b: She clarified the two facts rather than confusing them.
wrong.c: She did not substitute one fact for another.
wrong.d: She made the facts more visible, not hidden.

items.hint: She placed two facts together so the contrast would be obvious.
items.explanation: Setting record profits next to falling wages highlights the contrast: she juxtaposed them.
items.clue: letting the contrast make her argument

items.prompt: What does the director do in this scene?
items.passage: The film cuts directly from a feast in the king's palace, with tables overflowing, to a family outside the walls sharing a single loaf of bread.

options.text: The director juxtaposes wealth and poverty.

items.hint: Two opposite scenes appear back-to-back.
items.explanation: Cutting straight from the feast to the single loaf places the scenes side by side, juxtaposing wealth and poverty to highlight the gap.
items.clue: cuts directly from... to

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what juxtapose means.

chunks.text: The textbook
juxtaposes two maps of Europe
on facing pages, one from 1914 and one from 1919.
in separate chapters, hundreds of pages apart.

items.hint: Juxtaposing places things side by side.
items.explanation: Maps on facing pages are side by side for easy comparison. Maps hundreds of pages apart are not juxtaposed.

items.prompt: Which speaker uses "juxtapose" correctly?

options.text: "I juxtaposed my bike down the hill really fast."
"She juxtaposed a glass of water because she was thirsty."
"If you juxtapose the two essays, you can see how much stronger the second draft is."

items.hint: Juxtapose means place side by side to compare.
items.explanation: Placing two drafts side by side to compare them is juxtaposing. The other lines use the word for riding, drinking, or taking out trash.

words.definition: ordinary, routine, and unexciting

hero.text: Between dramatic rescues, Nova spends hours on mundane tasks like filling out reports and cleaning her gear.

words.everyday: The documentary showed the mundane daily life of astronauts: exercising, fixing equipment, and cleaning filters.
